Malicious

muh-LISH-us — contains 'mal,' meaning bad; malicious acts come from a bad, harmful intent. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Malicious is intended or meant to cause harm.

The company traced the malicious software back to a hacker who wanted to steal customer data.

Worked Example

A student, jealous of a classmate's success, spreads a false story about her online purely to embarrass her in front of the whole school, with no real disagreement or grievance behind it at all.

Deliberately trying to hurt someone for no real reason other than the desire to cause harm is malicious. Unlike 'careless,' which is accidental, malicious behavior is intentional and meant to wound.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

spiteful: showing a desire to hurt or upset someone

vindictive: having a strong desire for revenge

malevolent: having or showing a wish to do harm

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

benevolent: well-meaning and kind

harmless: not able or likely to cause harm

Where it sits · how deliberate and cruel the harm is — unkind → malicious → vicious

unkind vs. malicious: Unkind is weaker than malicious — being unkind can be thoughtless, while malicious behavior is deliberately and specifically meant to cause harm.

vicious vs. malicious: Vicious is stronger than malicious: malicious behavior is intended to harm, but vicious adds real cruelty and violence to that intent.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — mal-

root — mal-: bad, evil (Latin)

suffix — -icious

suffix — -icious: full of, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin malitia ('badness, ill will') comes from malus, meaning 'bad.' Malicious describes behavior that is, at its root, full of bad intent toward someone.

Use the root in a new word: malfunction

Use the root in a new word: malfunction: The elevator suffered a sudden malfunction and stopped working between floors.
